cases.title: Profitable pharmacy software vendor, price down on a cloud transition
reasons: Kill criteria: none met. Net debt/EBITDA is 0.3x, well below the 4x limit. No holder above 25%, so there is no controlling shareholder who ruled out a sale. The facts state no regulatory issue, so there is no unresolved regulatory or data-privacy problem.
Segment: pharmacy software is a preferred segment. It is not RCM-only.

Business model: recurring revenue is 78% of sales, above the 50% threshold. Churn is under 3%, which points to sticky customers and high switching costs. The EBITDA margin is 21%, so the company is profitable.

Why the price is low: the share fell 30% over 12 months (-8% over 3 months). The cause is a temporary cloud migration of the customer base that depressed license revenue, and management expects it to complete next year. This is a cloud-transition dip, not a structural loss of customers or share. The thesis names this as acceptable.

Ownership flag (flag only): the top holder is Lambert Family Office at 14%, and insiders hold 15%. Both are below the 25% flag threshold, so nothing is triggered. The data has no public statements about selling.

Fit: this closely matches the thesis's good-fit example, which is a profitable pharmacy software vendor with mostly subscription revenue, little net debt and a share price down after a cloud-transition dip. The only difference is that the family stake is smaller than the large stake in that example. That is not a criterion.
Actionable status is not part of this verdict. The code decides it by comparing the takeout price with the target price.

cases.title: Healthcare IT services, recurring revenue 38%
reasons: No kill criterion is met. Net debt/EBITDA is 0.8x (below 4x). No holder is above 25% (top holder Davy Asset Management at 8%, insiders 10%), so there is no ownership flag and no sale has been ruled out. The facts report no regulatory issue.

Segment fit: this is a services business that does project-based implementation and integration for medtech software. It is not a software vendor in the EHR, pharmacy, healthcare analytics, pharma software or medtech software segments we like. The thesis wants software with high switching costs, and this business sells services. Outside the liked segments, the thesis rule gives Radar.

Business model (warning only, does not lower the verdict): recurring support contracts are 38% of sales, below the 50% threshold. The revenue is mainly project-based, which is not the sticky, subscription-like profile we want.

Other points: EBITDA margin of 12% is modest for the profile we target. Net debt is low, and market cap of EUR 300m is a manageable size. These do not change the verdict.

Conclusion: the price drop looks temporary and the balance sheet is clean, but the company is outside our preferred segments and has low recurring revenue. We keep it on the watchlist and do not make it a Priority.

The other kill criteria are not met. Net debt/EBITDA is 0.9x, below the 4x limit. No holder is above 25%, so there is no controlling shareholder who has ruled out a sale.

The company otherwise fits the strategy. It is an EHR vendor, which is a preferred segment. Recurring revenue is 82% of sales, above the 50% bar. EBITDA margin is 22%, and the share price is down 18% over 3 months and 40% over 12 months. The data-privacy kill criterion takes precedence over this fit.
Ownership flag: no holder is above 25%. The top holder is Nordea Asset Management at 7%, and insiders hold 9%. Nothing is flagged and no sale statements are reported.
Whether the price drop is temporary is unclear. It may be linked to the incident, but the facts do not say so. This does not change the verdict because the kill criterion already decides it.
